lessonTitle: Paroxysmal Neurology: Seizure versus Syncope, Status Epilepticus and Headache

blocks.text: A 30-year-old man is found on the pavement by a passer-by who says he went stiff, jerked for two minutes and then lay confused. A paramedic arrives and wants to know: was this a seizure or a faint? The answer lies almost entirely in the history and in what the witness saw, because the examination between attacks is usually normal.

blocks.markdown: Many neurological emergencies are **paroxysmal**: sudden, brief and followed by recovery. The commonest transient loss of consciousness (TLoC) mechanisms are **syncope** (global cerebral hypoperfusion), **epileptic seizure** (abnormal synchronous neuronal discharge) and functional (psychogenic) events. A **seizure** is the clinical manifestation of that discharge; **epilepsy** is a tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures. Syncope is usually reflex (vasovagal, situational), orthostatic (postural fall in blood pressure) or cardiac (arrhythmia or structural disease, which is the dangerous group). Because first-line tests are often normal, the diagnosis is made from the story, with an ECG and lying and standing blood pressure in every patient.

rows: Often none; sleep deprivation, alcohol withdrawal, flashing lights
Possible aura (rising epigastric sensation, deja vu, smell)
Stiffening then rhythmic jerking, cyanosis, eyes open, head turning
Post-ictal confusion for minutes to hours; headache and aching muscles
blocks.caption: History and witness features that separate syncope from epileptic seizure. Brief myoclonic jerks can occur in syncope, so jerking alone does not prove a seizure.

blocks.title: Weighing the witness account
blocks.prompt: A 17-year-old stands up quickly in a hot lecture hall, feels faint, sees dark at the edges of vision, sweats and slumps. A friend says she was pale for about 20 seconds, jerked her arms briefly, then woke fully orientated within a minute. What is the likely cause?

steps.text: Identify trigger and prodrome: standing in a hot room, with tunnel vision and sweating before collapse. This favours syncope.
Identify the event: pale and limp, with brief unresponsiveness of 20 seconds. Brief jerks after loss of consciousness are common in syncope (convulsive syncope).
Identify the recovery: rapid, with full orientation. Prolonged post-ictal confusion would suggest seizure.
Next steps: ECG and lying-standing blood pressure to exclude a cardiac or orthostatic cause.

blocks.answer: Reflex (vasovagal) syncope with convulsive features, not epilepsy.

blocks.title: Status epilepticus
blocks.text: Status epilepticus is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, or two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between them. It is a medical emergency with risk of hypoxia, aspiration and permanent brain injury, and the aim is to stop the seizure promptly.

items: Airway, breathing and circulation: place in recovery position, give high-flow oxygen, secure IV access, and check capillary glucose (treat hypoglycaemia).

First-line benzodiazepine: IV lorazepam (teaching example: adults 4 mg; children 0.1 mg/kg), which may be repeated once after 10 minutes. If there is no IV access, buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam can be used.

If seizures continue after two benzodiazepine doses, give a second-line antiseizure drug as an IV infusion: levetiracetam or phenytoin are the usual choices (phenytoin loading dose 20 mg/kg at no more than 50 mg/min with ECG monitoring, teaching example). Sodium valproate is an option only with a caveat: under MHRA advice it must not be used in girls and women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated and the conditions of the pregnancy prevention programme are met. All doses here are teaching examples: check against current BNF, NICE and local guidance.
If still refractory, escalate to intensive care and general anaesthesia.
Look for the cause: alcohol withdrawal (give thiamine), hypoglycaemia, electrolytes, infection, structural lesion, drug non-adherence.

blocks.title: Weight-based benzodiazepine dose
blocks.prompt: A convulsing 14 kg child has IV access. Using the paediatric teaching dose of lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, calculate the dose.

steps.text: Multiply the weight by the dose per kilogram.
Check against the usual adult maximum of 4 mg; 1.4 mg is well below it.
If the seizure persists after 10 minutes, repeat once, then move to a second-line agent.

blocks.markdown: **Headache.** Most headaches are primary and benign, but a few are secondary to dangerous disease. **Red flags** include a sudden (thunderclap) onset reaching maximum within a minute, new onset over age 50, systemic features (fever, weight loss, malignancy, immunosuppression), focal neurological signs, papilloedema, a change in the usual pattern, headache worse lying flat or with Valsalva, and jaw claudication or scalp tenderness. Thunderclap headache suggests subarachnoid haemorrhage and needs an urgent non-contrast CT head (and lumbar puncture if CT is normal and suspicion persists, per local guidance). A new headache in a patient over 50 with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and a high ESR or CRP is giant cell arteritis, and high-dose corticosteroid is started immediately to prevent blindness, before temporal artery confirmation.

rows: 4 to 72 hours; nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, worse with movement; aura in about a third (visual, lasting 5 to 60 minutes)
Simple analgesia or NSAID, triptan, antiemetic
Bilateral, pressing or band-like, mild to moderate
30 minutes to days; no nausea, not worsened by activity
15 to 180 minutes, once to several times daily in bouts; tearing, red eye, nasal congestion, ptosis, restlessness
blocks.caption: Primary headache disorders compared.

blocks.title: Medication overuse
blocks.text: Frequent use of simple analgesics or triptans (on more than about 10 to 15 days per month) can itself cause a chronic daily headache. Always ask how many days a month acute medication is taken.

points: Distinguish seizure from syncope using trigger, prodrome, witness description, duration, tongue biting and recovery.
Status epilepticus is a seizure of 5 minutes or longer; treat with ABC, glucose, IV lorazepam, then a second-line antiseizure drug.
Headache red flags include thunderclap onset, age over 50 at onset, fever, focal signs and papilloedema.
Migraine, tension-type and cluster headaches differ in laterality, duration and associated features.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man taking tamsulosin and a thiazide diuretic gets up quickly from bed at night to pass urine, feels lightheaded and collapses. His wife says he was pale and limp for about 15 seconds and then was fully alert. Blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg lying and 100/58 mmHg after 3 minutes standing. What is the most likely cause?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: postural fall in blood pressure with drugs that lower it, brief pallor and rapid recovery.
distractorRationale.b: A tonic-clonic seizure would have prolonged confusion afterwards.
distractorRationale.c: Focal seizures do not typically have a postural prodrome and rapid recovery.

questions.explanation: The collapse follows standing, with a large postural fall in blood pressure on two vasoactive drugs, and recovery is rapid and complete, which is the pattern of orthostatic syncope. An ECG is still performed to exclude a cardiac cause, and the offending medication is reviewed.

questions.stem: Which witness-reported feature best favours an epileptic seizure over syncope?

options.text: Lateral tongue biting with 20 minutes of confusion afterwards
Pallor and sweating before the event
Collapse on standing from a chair

questions.correctOptionText: Lateral tongue biting with 20 minutes of confusion afterwards

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lateral tongue bite and prolonged post-ictal confusion indicate seizure.

questions.explanation: Lateral tongue biting and prolonged post-ictal confusion are the most specific features of a generalised seizure. Postural triggers, a prodrome of sweating and pallor and rapid recovery all favour syncope.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has been convulsing for 6 minutes without regaining consciousness. Oxygen is on, capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L, and IV access is established. What is the next drug?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: IV benzodiazepine is first-line in status epilepticus.
distractorRationale.b: Oral drugs are inappropriate in a convulsing patient.
distractorRationale.d: Propofol and anaesthesia are used for refractory status.

questions.explanation: A seizure lasting beyond 5 minutes is status epilepticus, and after airway, oxygen and glucose checks the first drug is an intravenous benzodiazepine, repeated once if needed. Second-line drugs are only used if seizures continue after two doses.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a sudden, severe headache that reached maximum intensity within one minute while lifting, with neck stiffness. Examination is otherwise normal. What is the most appropriate first investigation?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: thunderclap onset suggests subarachnoid haemorrhage, detected on CT.
distractorRationale.b: Blood cultures do not address the suspected diagnosis.
distractorRationale.d: Temporal artery biopsy is for suspected giant cell arteritis.

questions.explanation: Thunderclap headache is a red flag for subarachnoid haemorrhage, and non-contrast CT is highly sensitive for blood in the first hours. If CT is normal but suspicion persists, lumbar puncture is considered according to local guidance.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has attacks of severe pain behind the right eye lasting 45 minutes, up to three times nightly for 5 weeks, with a red, watering eye and nasal blockage. He paces the room. What is the best acute treatment?

options.text: Oral paracetamol and rest in a dark room
Propranolol taken at the start of an attack

distractorRationale.a: Correct: oxygen (or subcutaneous sumatriptan) aborts cluster headache.
distractorRationale.b: Simple analgesia is too slow for cluster headache.
distractorRationale.d: Propranolol is not an acute treatment for cluster headache.

questions.explanation: Brief, severe, strictly unilateral periorbital pain with autonomic features and restlessness in bouts is cluster headache. Oxygen and subcutaneous triptans act within minutes, unlike oral simple analgesics.

questions.stem: A convulsing 22 kg child is given IV lorazepam at the paediatric teaching dose of 0.1 mg/kg. Calculate the dose in mg.
questions.explanation: Dose = 0.1 mg/kg x 22 kg = 2.2 mg, which is below the adult dose of 4 mg. It may be repeated once after 10 minutes if seizures continue.

questions.stem: A 75 kg adult in status epilepticus has continued seizing after two doses of lorazepam. Calculate the phenytoin loading dose at 20 mg/kg (teaching example) in mg.
questions.explanation: Loading dose = 20 mg/kg x 75 kg = 1500 mg. At a maximum infusion rate of 50 mg/min this takes at least 30 minutes with ECG and blood pressure monitoring, which is why levetiracetam is often preferred (valproate is restricted in girls and women of childbearing potential under MHRA advice). Check doses against current BNF, NICE and local guidance.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old collapses at a railway station. Explain how you would use the history and the witness account to separate epileptic seizure from syncope, and name the bedside tests you would perform for syncope.
markingGuide: Triggers and prodrome: standing, heat, pain and lightheadedness favour syncope; aura favours seizure
Appearance: pallor and limpness in syncope; stiffening, rhythmic jerking, cyanosis, head turning in seizure
Duration: seconds in syncope, minutes in seizure
Recovery: rapid in syncope, post-ictal confusion in seizure
Brief jerks can occur in syncope
Bedside tests: ECG and lying and standing blood pressure
Cardiac syncope features: exertion, palpitations, family history of sudden death
questions.explanation: The examination between events is usually normal, so the diagnosis depends on the story. Syncope is caused by transient hypoperfusion and recovers quickly, while seizures produce characteristic motor features and prolonged post-ictal recovery.

questions.stem: Describe the emergency management of a 35-year-old man with convulsive status epilepticus, including the second-line options and possible causes you should look for.
markingGuide: Definition: seizure of 5 minutes or longer or recurrent seizures without recovery
Airway, breathing, circulation, high-flow oxygen, recovery position
Check capillary glucose and give glucose if low
IV access and IV lorazepam, repeat once after 10 minutes if needed
Buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam if no IV access

Second-line: levetiracetam or phenytoin as the usual options (sodium valproate only with the MHRA caveat: not for girls and women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated and pregnancy prevention programme conditions are met)
Causes: alcohol withdrawal (thiamine), hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance, infection, structural brain lesion, missed antiseizure drugs
questions.explanation: Prolonged seizures cause hypoxia and neuronal injury, so treatment is escalated quickly in a fixed sequence. At the same time reversible causes such as hypoglycaemia and alcohol withdrawal are corrected.

questions.stem: True or false: tension-type headache is typically a unilateral throbbing pain accompanied by nausea and worsened by routine physical activity.
questions.explanation: Tension-type headache is bilateral, pressing or band-like and mild to moderate, without nausea or worsening with activity. The description given fits migraine.
